name: MindBridge LucidFrame Dream Capture Implant
body_location: cranial — bilateral temporal lobe electrode array with subdermal transmitter behind right ear
description:
The LucidFrame operates by passively monitoring neural oscillation patterns during REM sleep, identifying the signature waveforms of active dream states and encoding them as structured experiential data. Thin-film electrode arrays distributed across the temporal and occipital lobes capture the raw sensory and emotional content of dreams — visual, auditory, and affective channels — compressing them into a proprietary MindBridge format called a .lux file. The implant stores up to 90 hours of dream content onboard before requiring an offload via the MindBridge companion app, which renders dreams as immersive playback experiences. It does not influence or direct dreams; it only records them, though a premium firmware tier called LucidFrame Guided offers gentle environmental audio cues to encourage dream continuity.

For most people who get the LucidFrame, the motivation is simple: they've had a dream they desperately wanted to remember and couldn't. Artists use it as a creative reservoir, scrubbing back through weeks of subconscious imagery for visual reference or emotional texture. Parents share cleaned and edited dream clips with their children like home videos. Couples exchange dreams the way they once exchanged playlists. There's an enormous gray market of dream content — anonymous uploads of vivid shared experiences, nightmare tourism, and curated emotional archives. On the Shelf, where entertainment options are scarce, a secondhand LucidFrame with a cracked offload port is still one of the most coveted consumer implants a teenager can own.
installation_requirements: Outpatient neural clinic; 90-minute procedure under local anesthetic; follow-up calibration appointment at 2 weeks
maintenance: Annual firmware update recommended; offload cache every 30-90 days via companion app; electrode array inspection every 2 years

side_effects: Heightened dream vividness and emotional intensity during first 3-4 weeks of calibration
Occasional difficulty distinguishing very recent dreams from real memories upon waking
Mild pressure sensation behind right ear near transmitter site, typically fades within 6 weeks
Some users report a subjective sense of 'performing' for the implant, causing temporary insomnia
cultural_context: Dream recording has become one of the defining social rituals of the 2180s and 2190s, and the LucidFrame is the implant most associated with that shift. Among Tier 2 and 3 users, sharing a dream with someone carries genuine intimacy — it's considered more vulnerable than sharing a journal, and some couples treat mutual dream-sharing as a relationship milestone. There is a thriving subculture of dream critics and curators on the MindBridge social platform, rating and archiving notable uploads. On the Shelf, the culture is rawer: unedited nightmares circulate as a form of extreme content, and there's a well-documented underground market for the dreams of people who've experienced extreme trauma or euphoria. Corporate HR departments in Tier 4 and 5 have begun quietly noting whether job candidates have public dream profiles, though this practice exists in a legal gray zone. For most people, though, the LucidFrame is simply a diary that writes itself.
known_users: Artists, musicians, and writers mining subconscious imagery for creative work
Teenagers and young adults on the Shelf who use dream-sharing as social currency
Grieving individuals who hope to dream of deceased loved ones and preserve the experience
Therapists' patients using dream logs as supplementary mental health records
Amateur dream-tourism content creators with public archive feeds
story_hooks: A character's LucidFrame begins capturing dreams that don't belong to them — fragmented, distressing imagery from an unknown source bleeding into their nightly archive. Tracing the signal leads somewhere no one was supposed to find.
A recently deceased person's LucidFrame archive is discovered intact. Their family wants it preserved; a media corponation wants to license it; and someone in the dreams wants it destroyed.

A Tier 1 teenager is selling their dreams — specifically, their rare and extraordinarily vivid night terrors — to a gray-market distributor. The money is good. The cost is becoming something the market wants rather than a person.
